quote: Es entsteht nun die Frage, ob es Funktionen {+von $x,y,z$+} giebt, welche nicht dadurch erzeugt werden können, dass man in Funktionen von je 2 [-Parametern-] {+Argumenten+} einsetzt
english: The question now arises whether there are functions of x, y, z which cannot be generated by substituting into functions of two arguments each
topic: The page first sets an axiom that preferences form an ordered set, used to count the votes an assembly needs to choose among 8 possibilities. It then discusses d'Ocagne's nomographic claim about functions of 3 variables and asks whether there are functions of x, y, z that cannot be built by composing functions of two arguments.

triage.modern_statement: Superposition (nomography) problem: does there exist a function f(x,y,z) of three variables that can't be written as a finite composition (superposition) of functions of two variables, e.g. f = F(G(x,y), H(y,z)) and deeper nestings? The question only means something once a function class is fixed. With arbitrary functions it is trivial, because a bijection R^2 -> R lets every function be built this way. The real versions ask about continuous, smooth/C^k or algebraic functions. Hilbert later published it as his 13th Problem (1900): can the roots of the general 7th-degree equation, which depend on 3 parameters, be written as superpositions of continuous or algebraic functions of two variables? He conjectured the answer was 'no'.
triage.answered_by: Continuous version: answered 'no such functions exist' by A. N. Kolmogorov and V. I. Arnold in 1956–57. Arnold (1957, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 114:679–681) showed every continuous function of three variables is a superposition of continuous functions of two variables. Kolmogorov (1957) went further: one-variable continuous functions plus addition are enough. Smooth version: there ARE continuously differentiable functions of three variables that can't be built from C^1 functions of two variables (Vitushkin's work; the arXiv source below states the result but my search didn't confirm the attribution). Algebraic version (Hilbert's literal wording): still open. For example, the resolvent degree rd(n) is unknown for every n >= 6.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 13th problem asks whether every continuous function of three variables can be written as a superposition (composition) of continuous functions of two variables; it arose in the context of nomography.
The problem was first presented in the context of nomographic construction, i.e. building a function of several variables from functions of two variables.
Arnold 1957: 'On the representation of continuous functions of three variables as superpositions of continuous functions of two variables', Dokl Akad Nauk SSSR 114(4):679–681.
Hilbert conjectured the answer was 'no', but in 1957 Kolmogorov and his student Arnold gave a positive solution in the continuous case.
There are continuously differentiable functions of three variables that cannot be written as a superposition of continuously differentiable functions of two variables.
Progress on the algebraic form of Hilbert's 13th problem has been slow; the resolvent degree rd(n) remains open for every n >= 6.
The Kolmogorov–Arnold superposition theorem is still a research topic, e.g. in current neural-network work.

triage.why: The note matches Hilbert's 13th Problem: it is set in d'Ocagne's nomography and asks whether some functions of x, y, z can't be generated by substituting into functions of two arguments. Hilbert posed exactly this in his 1900 list. The continuous case was settled by Kolmogorov and Arnold in 1957, against Hilbert's expected answer. In the smooth case such non-representable functions do exist. The algebraic case, which is what Hilbert literally asked, is still open and actively studied (resolvent degree, essential dimension). The Kolmogorov–Arnold theorem is also still studied, including in neural-network approximation. The diary note doesn't say which function class Hilbert had in mind. Without a restriction the question is trivial, so I am reading it as the start of the 13th problem rather than a separate question.
